newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW -RABO SAYS CHINA FUTURE IN LOCAL FIRMS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -RABO SAYS CHINA FUTURE IN LOCAL FIRMS.

text.p: Dutch agri-finance giant Rabobank [RABN.CN] is looking to fund within the next two to five years increasingly competitive, wholly Chinese-owned food and agribusiness firms, a senior banker said on Tuesday.

"We hope that in the not too distant future we're going to be able to provide project finance for Chinese companies as well (as to joint ventures)," Roger Bradshaw, senior manager at Rabobank's agri-project finance team, told Reuters.
"We've identified a few Chinese companies we would like to talk to more seriously about project finance," Bradshaw said.
Much of Rabobank's business in China rested on joint ventures, but increasingly efficient Chinese firms provided a fount of future investment opportunity, Bradshaw said.
In the beer market for example, joint ventures had stolen the march in terms of advertising, distribution and packaging, but Chinese companies were fighting back and gaining ground, he said.
"We will see more Chinese companies looking to finance their investments coming to the international markets to do that," he said.
He said that Rabobank was interested in Chinese companies that had a focused business scope and a solid track record.

Rabobank invested in five projects in China in 1996, they expect at least eight to be completed in 1997 and forecast that number could almost double next year to between 12 and 15 projects, Bradshaw said.
"Over the next ten years, it wouldn't be hard to see a four- to five-fold increase in investment in agri-processing in China," Bradshaw said.

In China this year, Rabobank is providing debt to pig slaughtering and processing projects, poultry processing operations, compound feed mills, malting, and medium density fibre boards, with a range of other projects under appraisal.
Agricultural processing projects in China typically involved sums between US$12 and 50 million and usually the debt-equity ratio was equal, Bradshaw said.

Earlier problems investors faced with Chinese companies, such as a lack of transparency and obscure accounting practises, were gradually being solved, he said, adding that caution was still called for.
"So it's an area where we have to be fairly prudent in assessing the risk and the ability of the sponors to implement the project," Bradshaw said.

China needed investment in its pork and poultry processing and in its feed mills to meet booming domestic demand, fuelled by rising incomes and the resulting shift in food buying from wet markets to supermarkets.
"Basically pork production is a backyard production, what you will see in the coming years is a more integrated pork production in place," he said.
Chinese agriculture faced huge wastage from poor harvesting techiques, poor transportation, poor storage, and poor planning for feed mills, Bradshaw said.
